sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x e^x\,dx$ using integration by parts.
questions.answer: Let $u = x$, $dv = e^x\,dx$: $= xe^x - \int e^x\,dx = xe^x - e^x + C$.
questions.explanation: Let $u = x$, $dv = e^x\,dx$: $= xe^x - \int e^x\,dx = xe^x - e^x + C$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x\cos x\,dx$ using integration by parts.
questions.answer: Let $u = x$, $dv = \cos x\,dx$: $= x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C$.
questions.explanation: Let $u = x$, $dv = \cos x\,dx$: $= x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int \ln x\,dx$ using integration by parts (with $dv = dx$).
questions.answer: Let $u = \ln x$, $dv = dx$: $= x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$.
questions.explanation: Let $u = \ln x$, $dv = dx$: $= x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x^2 e^x\,dx$, applying integration by parts twice.
questions.answer: First pass ($u=x^2$): $x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$. Second pass gives $\int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - e^x$. Total: $x^2e^x - 2xe^x + 2e^x + C$.
questions.explanation: First pass ($u=x^2$): $x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$. Second pass gives $\int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - e^x$. Total: $x^2e^x - 2xe^x + 2e^x + C$.

questions.answer: Let $u=x$, $dv = e^{2x}dx$: $\left[\frac{x}{2}e^{2x} - \frac{1}{4}e^{2x}\right]_0^1 = \left(\frac{e^2}{2} - \frac{e^2}{4}\right) - \left(0 - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{e^2}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$.
questions.explanation: Let $u=x$, $dv = e^{2x}dx$: $\left[\frac{x}{2}e^{2x} - \frac{1}{4}e^{2x}\right]_0^1 = \left(\frac{e^2}{2} - \frac{e^2}{4}\right) - \left(0 - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{e^2}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x\ln x\,dx$, choosing $u=\ln x$ (logarithmic functions are prioritized as $u$ under the LIATE rule).
questions.answer: $u=\ln x$, $dv=x\,dx$, so $du=\frac{1}{x}dx$, $v=\frac{x^2}{2}$: $=\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int\frac{x^2}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^2}{4}+C$.
questions.explanation: $u=\ln x$, $dv=x\,dx$, so $du=\frac{1}{x}dx$, $v=\frac{x^2}{2}$: $=\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int\frac{x^2}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^2}{4}+C$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x^2\cos x\,dx$, applying integration by parts twice.
questions.answer: First: $u=x^2$, $dv=\cos x\,dx$: $x^2\sin x - 2\int x\sin x\,dx$. Second (on $\int x\sin x\,dx$): $=-x\cos x+\sin x$. Total: $x^2\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x + C$.
questions.explanation: First: $u=x^2$, $dv=\cos x\,dx$: $x^2\sin x - 2\int x\sin x\,dx$. Second (on $\int x\sin x\,dx$): $=-x\cos x+\sin x$. Total: $x^2\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x + C$.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Evaluate $\int e^x\sin x\,dx$ using the technique of applying integration by parts twice and solving algebraically for the original integral.
questions.answer: Let $I=\int e^x\sin x\,dx$. First pass ($u=\sin x$, $dv=e^x dx$): $I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx$. Second pass on the new integral ($u=\cos x$): $\int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x + \int e^x\sin x\,dx = e^x\cos x + I$. So $I = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I$, giving $2I = e^x(\sin x-\cos x)$, so $I=\frac{e^x(\sin x-\cos x)}{2}+C$.
questions.explanation: Let $I=\int e^x\sin x\,dx$. First pass ($u=\sin x$, $dv=e^x dx$): $I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx$. Second pass on the new integral ($u=\cos x$): $\int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x + \int e^x\sin x\,dx = e^x\cos x + I$. So $I = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I$, giving $2I = e^x(\sin x-\cos x)$, so $I=\frac{e^x(\sin x-\cos x)}{2}+C$.

questions.answer: $u=x$, $dv=\sin x\,dx$: $\left[-x\cos x+\sin x\right]_0^{\pi} = (-\pi\cos\pi+\sin\pi)-(0) = \pi$.
questions.explanation: $u=x$, $dv=\sin x\,dx$: $\left[-x\cos x+\sin x\right]_0^{\pi} = (-\pi\cos\pi+\sin\pi)-(0) = \pi$.

questions.answer: $u=\ln x$, $dv=x^2dx$: $\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\ln x - \frac{x^3}{9}\right]_1^e = \left(\frac{e^3}{3}-\frac{e^3}{9}\right)-\left(0-\frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{2e^3}{9}+\frac{1}{9} = \frac{2e^3+1}{9}$.
questions.explanation: $u=\ln x$, $dv=x^2dx$: $\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\ln x - \frac{x^3}{9}\right]_1^e = \left(\frac{e^3}{3}-\frac{e^3}{9}\right)-\left(0-\frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{2e^3}{9}+\frac{1}{9} = \frac{2e^3+1}{9}$.

questions.q: Use integration by parts with $u=x^n$, $dv=e^x dx$ to derive the reduction formula $\int x^ne^x\,dx = x^ne^x - n\int x^{n-1}e^x\,dx$.
questions.answer: $du=nx^{n-1}dx$, $v=e^x$: $\int x^ne^x\,dx = x^ne^x - \int e^x\cdot nx^{n-1}\,dx = x^ne^x - n\int x^{n-1}e^x\,dx$.
questions.explanation: $du=nx^{n-1}dx$, $v=e^x$: $\int x^ne^x\,dx = x^ne^x - \int e^x\cdot nx^{n-1}\,dx = x^ne^x - n\int x^{n-1}e^x\,dx$.

questions.q: Use the reduction formula above (applied twice) to evaluate $\int x^2e^x\,dx$, confirming it matches an earlier result.
questions.answer: $\int x^2e^x\,dx = x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$. Applying again: $\int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - \int e^x\,dx = xe^x-e^x$. Total: $x^2e^x-2(xe^x-e^x) = x^2e^x-2xe^x+2e^x+C$, matching the earlier double-integration-by-parts result.
questions.explanation: $\int x^2e^x\,dx = x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$. Applying again: $\int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - \int e^x\,dx = xe^x-e^x$. Total: $x^2e^x-2(xe^x-e^x) = x^2e^x-2xe^x+2e^x+C$, matching the earlier double-integration-by-parts result.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int \tan^{-1}x\,dx$ using integration by parts with $u=\tan^{-1}x$, $dv=dx$.
questions.target: Integration by parts with inverse trig functions

questions.q: Evaluate $\int x\sin^{-1}x\,dx$ using $u=\sin^{-1}x$, $dv=x\,dx$ (the resulting integral can be left in terms of a known antiderivative form).
questions.target: Integration by parts with inverse trig functions
questions.answer: $du=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}dx$, $v=\frac{x^2}{2}$: $=\frac{x^2}{2}\sin^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$, which requires a further trigonometric substitution to complete.
questions.explanation: $du=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}dx$, $v=\frac{x^2}{2}$: $=\frac{x^2}{2}\sin^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$, which requires a further trigonometric substitution to complete.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^{\pi/2}x\cos(2x)\,dx$ exactly, using integration by parts.
questions.answer: $u=x$, $dv=\cos(2x)dx$, $v=\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)$: $\left[\frac{x}{2}\sin(2x)\right]_0^{\pi/2}-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2x)\,dx=\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\pi-0\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left[-\frac{1}{2}\cos(2x)\right]_0^{\pi/2}=0-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.explanation: $u=x$, $dv=\cos(2x)dx$, $v=\frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)$: $\left[\frac{x}{2}\sin(2x)\right]_0^{\pi/2}-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2x)\,dx=\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\pi-0\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left[-\frac{1}{2}\cos(2x)\right]_0^{\pi/2}=0-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: For each integral, state whether substitution or integration by parts is the appropriate technique, and identify the key choice ($u$-substitution variable, or $u$/$dv$ for parts) without fully evaluating: (a) $\int xe^{x^2}\,dx$; (b) $\int xe^{2x}\,dx$.
questions.cross_lesson: 3.02 Differentiation Rules: Power, Product, Quotient, Chain
questions.answer: (a) Substitution — $u=x^2$ makes $du=2x\,dx$ appear directly, no product rule needed. (b) Integration by parts — $x$ and $e^{2x}$ are genuinely different function types with no simplifying substitution; use $u=x$, $dv=e^{2x}dx$.
questions.explanation: (a) Substitution — $u=x^2$ makes $du=2x\,dx$ appear directly, no product rule needed. (b) Integration by parts — $x$ and $e^{2x}$ are genuinely different function types with no simplifying substitution; use $u=x$, $dv=e^{2x}dx$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int \sec^3x\,dx$ using integration by parts with $u=\sec x$, $dv=\sec^2x\,dx$, and the identity $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$ to solve the resulting equation for the original integral.
questions.answer: $du=\sec x\tan x\,dx$, $v=\tan x$: $I=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x\tan^2x\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x(\sec^2x-1)\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec^3x\,dx+\int\sec x\,dx$. So $2I=\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|$, giving $I=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|\right)+C$.
questions.explanation: $du=\sec x\tan x\,dx$, $v=\tan x$: $I=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x\tan^2x\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x(\sec^2x-1)\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec^3x\,dx+\int\sec x\,dx$. So $2I=\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|$, giving $I=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|\right)+C$.

questions.q: A city's population growth rate is modeled by $r(t)=t\ln(t+1)$ thousand people per year, for $0\leq t\leq5$. Set up and evaluate the definite integral for the total population growth over these 5 years using integration by parts, giving your answer to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Total growth $=\int_0^5 t\ln(t+1)\,dt$. This does not integrate cleanly with $u=\ln(t+1)$, $dv=t\,dt$ alone; using $u=\ln(t+1)$, $dv=t\,dt$, $v=\frac{t^2}{2}$: $\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\ln(t+1)\right]_0^5-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^5\frac{t^2}{t+1}\,dt$. Dividing $\frac{t^2}{t+1}=t-1+\frac{1}{t+1}$: $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^5\left(t-1+\frac{1}{t+1}\right)dt=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{t^2}{2}-t+\ln(t+1)\right]_0^5=\frac{1}{2}(12.5-5+\ln6)\approx4.65$. So total growth $\approx\frac{25}{2}\ln6-4.65\approx22.41-4.65\approx17.76$ thousand people.
questions.explanation: Total growth $=\int_0^5 t\ln(t+1)\,dt$. This does not integrate cleanly with $u=\ln(t+1)$, $dv=t\,dt$ alone; using $u=\ln(t+1)$, $dv=t\,dt$, $v=\frac{t^2}{2}$: $\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\ln(t+1)\right]_0^5-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^5\frac{t^2}{t+1}\,dt$. Dividing $\frac{t^2}{t+1}=t-1+\frac{1}{t+1}$: $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^5\left(t-1+\frac{1}{t+1}\right)dt=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{t^2}{2}-t+\ln(t+1)\right]_0^5=\frac{1}{2}(12.5-5+\ln6)\approx4.65$. So total growth $\approx\frac{25}{2}\ln6-4.65\approx22.41-4.65\approx17.76$ thousand people.

questions.answer: Final Answer: $0$ and $1$. Applying Applications of Integration principles, $x=x^2\Rightarrow x(x-1)=0$. Therefore, the verified correct option is $0$ and $1$.
questions.explanation: Applying Applications of Integration principles, $x=x^2\Rightarrow x(x-1)=0$. Therefore, the verified correct option is $0$ and $1$.

questions.q: State the formula for integration by parts.
questions.answer: Derived from the product rule: $\frac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv' \Rightarrow \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.
questions.explanation: Derived from the product rule: $\frac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv' \Rightarrow \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.

questions.answer: $u = x, dv = e^{2x}dx \Rightarrow du = dx, v = \frac{1}{2}e^{2x}$. $\int x e^{2x}dx = \frac{1}{2}x e^{2x} - \frac{1}{2}\int e^{2x}dx = \frac{1}{2}x e^{2x} - \frac{1}{4}e^{2x} + C$.
questions.explanation: $u = x, dv = e^{2x}dx \Rightarrow du = dx, v = \frac{1}{2}e^{2x}$. $\int x e^{2x}dx = \frac{1}{2}x e^{2x} - \frac{1}{2}\int e^{2x}dx = \frac{1}{2}x e^{2x} - \frac{1}{4}e^{2x} + C$.

questions.answer: $u = x, dv = \sin x dx \Rightarrow du = dx, v = -\cos x$. $uv - \int v\,du = -x\cos x - \int(-\cos x)dx = -x\cos x + \sin x + C$.
questions.explanation: $u = x, dv = \sin x dx \Rightarrow du = dx, v = -\cos x$. $uv - \int v\,du = -x\cos x - \int(-\cos x)dx = -x\cos x + \sin x + C$.

questions.answer: $u = \ln x, dv = dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{1}{x}dx, v = x$. $x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}dx = x\ln x - x + C$.
questions.explanation: $u = \ln x, dv = dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{1}{x}dx, v = x$. $x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}dx = x\ln x - x + C$.

questions.answer: $u = \arctan x, dv = dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{dx}{1+x^2}, v = x$. $x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C$.
questions.explanation: $u = \arctan x, dv = dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{dx}{1+x^2}, v = x$. $x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C$.

questions.answer: $u = \ln x, dv = x dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{dx}{x}, v = \frac{x^2}{2}$. $\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int \frac{x}{2}dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^2}{4} + C$.
questions.explanation: $u = \ln x, dv = x dx \Rightarrow du = \frac{dx}{x}, v = \frac{x^2}{2}$. $\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int \frac{x}{2}dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^2}{4} + C$.

questions.answer: Wallis: $\frac{5}{6}\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{5\pi\cdot3}{6\cdot4\cdot2\cdot2}=\frac{15\pi}{96}=\frac{5\pi}{32}$. Actually Wallis: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n}x\,dx=\frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2n)!!}\frac{\pi}{2}$.
